title: Sales Territory Radius Planner: Hub Coverage
description: Plan sales territories by radius from a hub with the Sales Territory Radius Planner — fair sizes, honest reach, before road refinement. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a territory of 500 square miles drawn as a circle has a radius of 12.6 miles — the planner's answer when management asks 'how far will the rep actually have to drive?'
quick_answer: The Sales Territory Radius Planner defines territory size by distance from a sales hub — enter the hub and a radius, or the area you need, and see the territory's size on the map — fair circles first, roads later.

Slide a candidate hub and watch its circle swallow or strand the accounts that matter. Radius first, lease second.
'Within our service radius' becomes a drawn fact rather than a slogan — customers inside 12.6 miles of the hub are in, and the map can prove it.

A 25-mile hub circle around Chicago covers about 1,963 sq mi and takes in Oak Park (8.0 mi), Evanston (11.7) and Gary, Indiana (24.5) — while Naperville (28.4) and Joliet (33.7) sit outside. State lines do not bend circles.
1,000 sq mi ↔ radius 17.8 miles; 200 sq mi ↔ 8.0 miles. The square root is the whole trick: radius grows slowly while area gallops.

faq: How do I choose a fair radius?
Start from the target area or account load, convert with this planner, then compare across hubs. Equal areas are the fair baseline; account density adjusts from there.
Can two hubs share accounts in the overlap?
Policy decides; geometry reports. The planner shows the overlap plainly so the policy conversation happens with a map open.
What about a hub near the coast or border?
The circle still draws; half of it may be water or another country. Effective territory is the landward, legal part — the planner shows the circle, judgment trims it.
Both — European territories plan in km with the same square-root arithmetic.
The refined second pass: drive-time catchments bend with roads and traffic. Radius planning is the honest first draft both methods share.
As many as the plan has — draw them all and read overlaps and gaps off the combined picture.
The radius and hub are the territory's definition; note them and any map tool redraws it. Boundaries for contracts deserve the drawn-region method.
Radii are cheap to redraw — seasonal plans can carry seasonal radii, with the dates written next to them so nobody sells last summer's map.
